lesson.title: When Growth Hits a Ceiling: The Logistic Model
lesson.summary: Logistic growth describes how a population expands quickly while resources are abundant, then slows and levels off as it approaches the environment's carrying capacity.
lesson.body:
Exponential growth assumes a population can keep multiplying at the same per capita rate forever. That is a useful starting model, but no real environment offers unlimited food, space, water, or nesting sites. As a population grows, it eventually starts to run into those limits, and its growth rate has to change. The logistic growth model is the standard way ecologists capture that reality.

The logistic equation builds directly on the exponential one. Exponential growth is written dN/dt = rN, where N is population size, t is time, and r is the intrinsic rate of increase (births minus deaths per individual, under ideal conditions). The logistic model adds a single new term: dN/dt = rN(1 - N/K), where K is the carrying capacity, the maximum population size the environment can sustain.

That added term, (1 - N/K), is doing all the work. When the population N is small relative to K, N/K is close to zero, so (1 - N/K) is close to 1, and growth looks nearly exponential, fast and accelerating. As N climbs toward K, N/K approaches 1, so (1 - N/K) shrinks toward zero, and growth slows down. When N actually equals K, (1 - N/K) becomes exactly zero, which makes dN/dt zero too: the population stops growing and levels off. This is why logistic growth traces an S shaped curve on a graph of population size over time, rather than the ever steepening J shape of exponential growth.

A worked example makes this concrete. Suppose a population has an intrinsic growth rate r = 0.4 per year and a carrying capacity K = 1,000 individuals. At N = 100 (well below K), dN/dt = 0.4 x 100 x (1 - 100/1000) = 0.4 x 100 x 0.9 = 36 individuals added that year. At N = 500, exactly halfway to K, dN/dt = 0.4 x 500 x (1 - 500/1000) = 0.4 x 500 x 0.5 = 100 individuals added, the fastest growth in this example. At N = 900, close to carrying capacity, dN/dt = 0.4 x 900 x (1 - 900/1000) = 0.4 x 900 x 0.1 = 36 individuals. And at N = 1,000, dN/dt = 0.4 x 1000 x 0 = 0: growth has stopped entirely. Notice the pattern: growth rate is low when the population is small (few individuals reproducing, even though resources are plentiful), rises to a maximum near N = K/2, and then falls back toward zero as crowding sets in near K. That peak at roughly the halfway point is a real mathematical feature of the logistic equation, not just an example artifact.

It is worth being honest about the model's limits. Very few real populations track a perfectly smooth logistic curve. Many overshoot K before settling back down, some oscillate around it, and time lags between a resource getting scarce and a population actually responding can produce much messier trajectories than the clean S curve suggests. Still, the logistic model is the foundation for understanding density dependence, the idea that a population's own growth rate responds to how crowded it has become, which later chapters build on directly.
